Kids and sensitive patients

Dye-free medications for kids and people with MCAS.

When the medicine is right but the dyes, fillers or flavors in it aren't, a compounding pharmacy can often make a version without them. Here's how it works and how to ask for it.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 18, 2026

It's not always the medicine

Every tablet, capsule and liquid contains inactive ingredients along with the active drug: dyes for color, fillers and binders to hold a tablet together, preservatives, sweeteners and flavors. For most people they don't matter. For some, they do:

  • Children who react to certain dyes or flavors, or who simply refuse a medicine because of its taste.
  • People with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), who may react to dyes, fillers or preservatives in commercial products.
  • People with allergies or intolerances, for example to lactose, gluten-containing starches, corn, peanut oil or certain sugar alcohols.

What a compounding pharmacy can change

From your prescriber's prescription, we can often prepare the same active ingredient in a version that fits you:

  • Dye-free capsules and liquids.
  • A different filler in capsules, chosen to avoid the ingredient you react to.
  • Preservative-free or sugar-free liquids, when the medicine allows it. These may need refrigeration or have a shorter beyond-use date.
  • A flavor your child will take, or no added flavor at all.
  • A custom strength, including small steps up or down that commercial products don't offer.

Not every medication can be changed in every way. A pharmacist will check what's possible and talk with your prescriber if needed.

Common medications people ask about

For MCAS, prescribers often order medications like ketotifen, H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine, famotidine and montelukast, and sometimes low-dose naltrexone. For children, flavored, dye-free liquids are a common request for medicines that only come as tablets. See our MCAS page and the medication library for more.

How to ask for a dye-free version

  1. Make a list of what you react to. Include specific dyes (for example FD&C Red No. 40), fillers, preservatives and flavors, and what happened.
  2. Check the inactive ingredients of what you take now. They're on the package insert, or search the product on DailyMed, the National Library of Medicine's drug label site.
  3. Ask your prescriber to send the prescription to a compounding pharmacy and note "dye-free" or the ingredients to avoid.
  4. Call us. Tell us your sensitivities and we'll talk through ingredients with you and your prescriber before we make it.
Allergic reactions can be serious. If you or your child has swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing or a severe reaction after any medicine, get emergency care right away. Then tell your prescriber and pharmacist so it's recorded.
Compounding for MCAS Talk to a pharmacist

Common questions

Will a dye-free version work the same?

It contains the same active ingredient in the strength your prescriber orders. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved, so ask your prescriber whether a compounded version is right for you.

Does insurance cover dye-free compounded medicine?

Coverage for compounded medications varies by plan, and many don't cover them. Call us and we'll tell you the price before we make it.

Can you make vitamins or supplements dye-free?

Ask us. We also carry professional supplement brands, and many offer versions without common allergens.

This article is general information and not medical advice. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved and are not commercially manufactured products. Your prescriber decides what's right for you.
